The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) is sponsoring an experimental and analytical program to investigate heat transfer within rotating turbine blades.
The Pratt & Whitney 3D-TEACH CFD code was selected as the baseline code for modification to meet the needs of the program.
The 3D-TEACH code solves the general steady flow equation in cylindrical coordinates, using a two-equation k-epsilon turbulence model for closure.
The code represents curvilinear surfaces using a 'stair-step' approach, which can lead to inaccuracies in calculating wall shear stress and surface heat transfer.
The code uses a 'law of the wall' approach with wall functions to handle boundary layer flows, rather than resolving the viscous sublayer.
Modifications to the 3D-TEACH code for rotating flows included adding additional source terms to the momentum and turbulence equations to account for Coriolis and centrifugal forces.
The code was verified against three sets of experimental data: Moon's duct flow, Moore's aspect ratio study, and Metzger's sharp bend heat transfer experiment.
The comparisons showed the 3D-TEACH code could capture the major effects of rotation, but had some discrepancies in predicting fluctuating quantities and heat transfer in the sharp bend.

The main conclusions were that the 3D-TEACH code shows promise, but has limitations that need to be addressed through further improvements in turbulence modeling, grid generation, and numerical schemes.
Accurately predicting coolant-side heat transfer and pressure drop in turbine blades is important for improving reliability in predicting blade temperatures and life.

Key challenges in developing computational methods for rotating turbine blade passages include the complex turbulent flow, effects of rotation, and need to resolve boundary layers and intricate geometries.
The experimental program aims to generate a comprehensive database that can form the basis of an empirical design system, in addition to the computational modeling efforts.
The overall objective of the NASA program is to develop and verify improved analysis methods that will result in efficient turbine components with improved durability.
The computational fluid dynamics approach was selected due to the complexity of the flow within turbine blades, which makes comprehensive empirical correlations difficult to obtain.
The study is part of a larger NASA program that also includes experimental investigations and the development of a design system based on the combined experimental and computational results.
